question: Should the requiresUAT close gate keep demanding a walk (binary walked | waived), or demand a per-component accounting in which an attested 'no UAT' is a passing value?
decision: The gate stops demanding a walk and starts demanding an accounting. disposition.uat carries one facts-only record per component -- component, method, human reviewer type and count, evidence, findings, and an explicit attested none -- and coverage is checked against the spec's declared uatComponents inventory rather than against whatever records happen to be present. Method 'none' and 'not-applicable' PASS with an attestation; the only refusal is a declared component with no answer at all. No self-assessed confidence score and no parallel debt ledger.

options.option: Keep the Set 111 S4 binary walked | waived
options.consequence: Preserves the strongest form of the gate, but cannot express the operator's own worked example (watch the low-risk components, walk the high-risk ones), so the honest answer for a mixed session is unrecordable and the pressure is toward a blanket waiver. A near-100% waiver rate is a gate that has been routed around rather than satisfied.

options.option: Per-component accounting, gated on the spec's declared component inventory (chosen)
options.consequence: Nothing blocks on how much UAT was done, so the impasse objection is answered; nothing evaporates, because an in-scope component with no record still refuses the close. Strictly weaker as a forcing function and strictly stronger as a record. Costs spec authors one new required key (uatComponents) on armed sets, and is BREAKING for consumer repos holding a disposition in the old shape.

options.option: Per-component accounting, gated only on the records present
options.consequence: Cheapest to adopt and the one consult round 3 explicitly warned against: the disposition would declare both the question and the answer, so an omitted component becomes the new form of evaporation and the gate silently stops protecting the thing it was built for.

operator_attestation: Operator ruling, recorded in operator-notes.md 2026-08-10 and ruled accepted after the round-1 consults: "Rather than gating on UAT, we could simply record what kind of UAT (and by how many developers and/or business users) was done for each component addressed by a session. That's useful documentation." The operator's stated grounds: "requiresUAT is not really a requirement if it can be bypassed - and it always can be, and always should be, to prevent impasses." They accepted the record-completeness gate explicitly - "'No UAT' is a valid, attested, passing value" - and this is the operator exercising the verification-reduction carve-out. The orchestrator wrote the record; it did not make the call, and could not: the AI-authority attempt above was refused, which is correct.

extra.inventory_check_source: Consult round 3: a gate that merely validates whatever records exist makes an omitted component the new form of evaporation. Survived the round commissioned to attack the consensus.

question: This session's own gate refuses an armed set that declares no uatComponents inventory, and Set 113 is such a set. Does Session 1 add uatComponents to Set 113's own configuration block, given that the spec's configuration block is immutable at runtime?
decision: Add it, in this session, with an amendment note in the spec header. The immutability rule protects arming FLAGS from being re-litigated mid-session to change what a gate demands of the session running; uatComponents arms nothing, supplies data the new gate reads, and cannot affect Sessions 1-3, which owe no accounting under uatScope: per-set. The four entries are read off this spec's own Creates lines. Leaving it out would ship a gate that makes this set's own Session 4 unclosable by an author who had no way to know.

options.option: Add uatComponents now, with an amendment note (chosen)
options.consequence: Set 113 can close its own Session 4. Costs one spec edit that a strict reading of runtime immutability would question, so the reasoning is journaled and the spec header records it rather than the edit appearing unexplained.

options.option: Leave it to Session 4
options.consequence: Honours the immutability rule literally. Session 4 hits a close refusal for a key nobody told it about, at the most expensive moment in the set - the set-terminal close, after the OS-capture pilot. The rule would have protected nothing and cost a stranded close.

options.option: Make a missing inventory inert instead
options.consequence: No spec edit needed anywhere, and it guts the feature: an absent key would disarm the gate exactly where the author was least deliberate, which is the evaporation this session exists to close. Refused.

extra.immutability_rule: session-constitution.md: 'The spec's configuration block, as captured at set start, is immutable at runtime.' Read as protecting arming decisions, not as forbidding the data a newly-shipped gate reads.
extra.blast_radius: Set 113 is the only in-flight set in this repo and the only not-started set (134) declares requiresUAT: false, so no other spec in this repo needs the key today. Consumer repos do.

question: The full pytest suite went red with 9 failures the moment this session added its changelog fragment: the corpus was in the post-fold state (empty recorded baseline + foldedAt), nothing re-establishes a partition point on the first contribution after a release, and the changelog round-trip guard was therefore sitting disarmed. The gap is already named as queued work elsewhere. Fix it here, or stop and hand it to the operator?
decision: Fix exactly the post-fold transition and nothing else. add_fragment now calls _rebaseline_after_fold, which re-stamps the same three fields migrate stamps -- but ONLY when the baseline is in the post-fold empty state, treating the folded document as the new frozen history. A mid-cycle add is left untouched, preserving the behaviour every release before this one had. Two test-side re-seed guards that asked 'is the corpus empty' were corrected to ask 'does it hold two recorded fragments', which is what their planted-reorder falsifiers actually need. The WIDER question -- whether the round trip should cover pending fragments at all -- is deliberately NOT answered here and is flagged to the operator.

options.option: Fix only the post-fold transition (chosen)
options.consequence: Suite green, guard armed, changelog fragment kept. Adds ~40 lines to a module this session had no plan to touch, which is scope growth and is recorded as such. Changes nothing about what the guard proves mid-cycle.

options.option: Advance the round-trip pins on EVERY add
options.consequence: Closes the wider gap the queued set is about. REFUSED: it would re-stamp originalSha256 from the current file on every contribution, silently absorbing an edit to released history made just before one. That weakens what the guard proves, which is verification-reducing and not self-authorizable.

options.option: Drop the changelog fragment and close without it
options.consequence: Suite green with no code change at all. REFUSED: this session ships a BREAKING change for consumer repos, and the fragment carrying the symptom and the migration is the single most valuable artifact it produces for them.

options.option: Stop and ask the operator before touching anything
options.consequence: Most conservative. Costs a full session stop on a blocker that affects EVERY future session equally -- the next contributor after any release hits the identical red suite -- for a fix that turned out to be scoped and test-verifiable. The wider design question is escalated instead, which is the part that actually needs them.

extra.blast_radius: Not specific to this session. The corpus has been in the post-fold state since the 1.0.0 fold on 2026-08-15; this was the first contribution after it, so the first session to add any changelog fragment would have hit the same 9 failures.
extra.escalated_to_operator: Whether check() should round-trip PENDING fragments, not just recorded ones. Left open; it changes what the guard proves.
extra.post_verification_change: ai_router/changelog.py is shipped code changed after the VERIFIED round, so it owes one delta-scoped --phase remediation-review (A4). The two test-file changes owe nothing under the same rule.

question: Which surface should the one exemplary scenario describe -- the AI Work Explorer (an Electron surface this repo owns) or a web fixture matching the (a)-(d) audience the operator named as the real target?
decision: The AI Work Explorer, via `npm run walk`. The model's portability is carried by the driver quarantine, not by the exemplar's platform: the portable half of this scenario contains no selector and no Electron concept, and the same source shape renders identically for a web target. Three concrete reasons decide it. The Work Explorer is the only human-observable surface that exists in this repo today, so its expected results can be checked against shipped code and pinned fixtures rather than invented against an application nobody has written. Session 3's own Creates line already names 'one recorded web scenario' authored against the fixture web app it builds, so a web exemplar here would be authored twice and would duplicate rather than extend. And Session 4's dogfood needs exactly this scenario, against exactly this surface.

options.option: Author the exemplar against the AI Work Explorer
options.consequence: Every expected result is checkable against shipped code and the pinned uat-matrix fixtures, so the walkthrough is true on the day it ships. Session 4 gets its dogfood scenario for free. Costs: the exemplar's target is the platform the operator called the odd one out, and a reader could mistake the exemplar for the model's intended scope.

options.option: Author the exemplar against a web fixture
options.consequence: Matches the (a)-(d) audience directly. But no web fixture exists until Session 3 builds one, so the steps would describe an application that does not yet exist -- unverifiable prose in a document whose entire value is that a stranger can follow it -- and Session 3 would then author its own web scenario over the top.

options.option: Author two exemplars, one per platform
options.consequence: Refused by the spec's own non-goals: 'This builds the capability and exactly one exemplary scenario, not a library.' It also doubles the authoring cost, which the spec names as the expensive half.

extra.operator_note: operator-notes.md 2026-08-10, 'Electron/VS Code is the odd platform out, not the target', and its own read: 'The portable value is the step format, not the recorder ... If the complexity budget forces a cut, cut recorder generality before step-format generality.'
extra.mitigation: docs/walkthroughs/README.md states the format is target-agnostic and names the exemplar as one instance; the round conventions record the choice so verification does not spend a finding rediscovering it.

question: Should the scenario format ship a JSON Schema alongside the Python validator, the way disposition.json does?
decision: No. One validator, in Python, is the whole contract. Session 1 of this same set spent three of its five blocking findings on disposition.schema.json and its Python validator disagreeing about one file -- two independent expressions of one shape that drifted the moment either moved. A scenario is an authored source read by exactly one consumer (the renderers), so a second machine-readable expression buys editor autocomplete and costs a permanent parity obligation. Adding one later is cheap; removing one after consumer repos depend on it is not.

options.option: Python validator only
options.consequence: One source of truth for the shape. No parity test, no drift class. Authors get error messages that name the key and the fix, but no editor autocomplete.

options.option: Python validator plus a JSON Schema
options.consequence: Editors can complete and validate scenario.yaml. Costs a parity test in perpetuity and re-opens the exact defect class Session 1 paid three Majors for, on a surface with far fewer readers than disposition.json.

extra.precedent: Set 113 S1 verification rounds 1-2: three Majors, all parity between disposition.schema.json and the Python validator.

question: Should scenario_lint refuse to render when selector-shaped text is found in a scenario's portable half, or only warn?
decision: Warn. The lint is advisory at the renderer and asserted at the test suite. A pattern gate over free prose has a real false-positive surface -- the exemplar tripped one on its first pass, on '.vscode-test', a directory name shaped exactly like a CSS class -- and a renderer that refused to run over a sentence resembling CSS would be worked around by deleting the sentence rather than by moving the selector. The committed corpus is asserted clean by pytest, so the rule still bites where it can be reasoned about; what is left out is only the ability to block an author mid-edit. Nothing that existed before this session is weakened: the lint is new, and the strongest form of the check -- pytest over the committed tree -- ships armed.

options.option: Advisory warning, corpus asserted clean in pytest
options.consequence: An author sees the finding and decides. A genuine leak reaching the committed tree fails the suite. A false positive costs a rewording, not a blocked render.

options.option: Hard refusal at render time
options.consequence: No leak can ever be rendered. But every false positive blocks an author who is trying to write clearer prose, which is the route-around-the-gate failure this set exists to name -- and the natural workaround is to delete the sentence, making the document worse.

extra.observed_false_positive: prerequisites[1] flagged '.vscode-test'; reworded to the path-qualified form, which reads better anyway. Recorded in the scenario_lint module docstring rather than exempted.

question: Round 1 of this session's verification reviewed an EMPTY diff (the work had been committed first, and verify_session defaults to a working-tree-vs-HEAD diff). Its two findings correctly said 'you handed me nothing', but because the only path they could cite was spec.md, the Set 119 doc-only cap recorded both at Minor and the tool printed 'MINOR-ONLY ... effectively VERIFIED' with instructions to close. Should this session fix that hole in ai_router/verify_session.py, or record it and hand it on?
decision: Fix it here, minimally: assemble_evidence now raises EvidenceEmptyError when the bundle carries no diff and no untracked contents, and close_backstop handles it explicitly instead of reporting it as a route failure. NOT fixed by making the severity cap cleverer -- the cap is operator-attested and behaved correctly on the input it was given; the defect is that the input should never have been routed. The larger candidate fix -- changing verify_session's DEFAULT diff base to the session-derived pre-session ref, the way close_backstop already does -- is deliberately NOT taken here: it changes behaviour for every set on the most expensive path there is, and belongs in a session that can verify it as its own subject.

options.option: Fix it here, minimally (chosen)
options.consequence: Closes the hole now; blast radius measured at two shared test fixtures plus one close-path handler, all covered.

options.option: Record it and hand it on entirely
options.consequence: The hole stays open and the next session can silently self-certify.

options.option: Weaken the Set 119 doc-only severity cap
options.consequence: Attacks the wrong component: the cap is operator-attested and behaved correctly on the input it was given.

options.option: Also change verify_session's default diff base
options.consequence: Strictly better long-term, but changes every set's close path and needs its own verification. Deferred, not rejected.

rationale: This is a verification-INCREASING change, so it is outside the human-only carve-out (which covers reductions). The class was already known and already fixed at ONE site: close_backstop derives its base from the session's startedAt precisely because 'a plain HEAD diff at close time is empty -- it would hand the verifier nothing', and fails closed rather than route a thin bundle. The interactive path never got the same treatment, which is G-008 / L-069-1 exactly: a point-fix reads complete while the class stays alive at the sibling, invisible until something exercises it. This session exercised it. Deferring to the gate that already exists -- and making it exist on the path that lacked it -- is the tiebreak that decided this. Blast radius was measured rather than assumed: two shared test fixtures were pristine trees, which meant every run() test had been exercising the routing and verdict logic over an empty bundle; both now carry one uncommitted change. 461 tests green across the verify_session, phases, backstop and walkthrough suites.

question: Cross-provider verification found that the recorder required a repository-local .venv. Should the fix be to document that prerequisite, or to remove the requirement?
decision: Remove the requirement, then document what is left. The recorder now accepts any interpreter that can actually import ai_router -- DABBLER_PYTHON, then the repo venv, then python3/python on PATH -- and verifies each candidate by importing rather than by checking that a file exists.

options.option: Remove the .venv requirement, then document what is left (chosen)
options.consequence: The recorder works in a consumer repo that pip-installed the router and has no repo venv.

options.option: Document the .venv prerequisite only
options.consequence: Satisfies the finding's letter while leaving the recorder usable in exactly one checkout.

rationale: The finding's acceptance criterion said 'without depending on an UNDOCUMENTED .venv', which documenting alone would have satisfied. But the goal behind it is that this capability is cross-cutting: consumer repos install dabbler-ai-router from PyPI and may have no repo-local virtualenv at all, so a hard .venv requirement would have made the recorder work in exactly one checkout -- this one -- while passing the letter of the criterion. Satisfying the letter would have left the spec's 'lands in shared infrastructure so consumer repos inherit it' false.

question: Verification found the generated index shows no captions over file://, which is the documented way to open it. Fix by serving the run directory, or by changing how captions get into the page?
decision: Change how they get in. The caption sidecar ELEMENT is gone; the cues are embedded in the page and added through the standard addTextTrack / VTTCue API on load, so the browser renders them with its own native caption UI and nothing is fetched. captions.vtt is still written and still listed as an artifact -- it is what you upload beside a copy of the video.

options.option: Embed the cues and build the track in-page (chosen)
options.consequence: Native captions over file://; removes a component instead of adding one.

options.option: Serve the run directory over HTTP to view it
options.consequence: Adds a process, a port and a lifecycle to a static deliverable whose point is opening off disk.

rationale: Requiring a web server to read a local file would have added a process, a port and a lifecycle to a static deliverable whose whole point is that it opens off disk. Building the track removes a failure mode instead of adding a component, and it removes the element rather than adding a fallback beside it (G-005). Verified empirically over file://: one track, kind captions, mode showing, five cues, the right cue active at 20s, and no console errors.

question: Probing the environment before the first capture found that the operator's default OBS scene collection carries a live webcam (NexiGo N940P), a microphone and Desktop Audio, plus a background-removal plugin. Should the fixed pass criteria be amended to forbid those source kinds, given that criteria decided after the first capture are not criteria?
decision: Amend C6 and C7 now, before any capture. C7's forbidden input kinds grow beyond screen capture to include camera and audio inputs (dshow_input, wasapi_input_capture, wasapi_output_capture, wasapi_process_output_capture), and the harness must assert its scene contains EXACTLY the one window-capture source it created. C6 grows a restore obligation for the obs-websocket config file. The amendment is legitimate because NO capture has been taken: the spec's bar is that criteria precede the first capture, not that they precede environment discovery. Recording the amendment and its cause is what keeps that claim checkable.

options.option: Amend now, before the first capture, and record why.
options.consequence: The criteria stay honest to their own rule and the operator's camera is asserted out of frame rather than assumed out of frame.

options.option: Leave the criteria as committed and rely on the dedicated scene collection to keep the webcam out.
options.consequence: An unasserted safety property is a hope, and this one is the operator's camera. Rejected.

options.option: Record it as a post-hoc caveat in the outcome.
options.consequence: Exactly the 'criteria decided after the first capture' failure the spec names. Rejected outright.

evidence: OBS log 2026-08-15 20-26-55.txt records the webcam, Mic/Aux and Desktop Audio sources initialising from the operator's existing scene collection.

question: OBS honours --websocket_port and --websocket_password but neither flag ENABLES the websocket server, which is disabled in the operator's obs-websocket config. Enabling it is a GUI action. May this session toggle that one boolean in the operator's config file to run the pilot?
decision: Yes, with the file backed up and restored byte-for-byte as part of C6's deterministic cleanup, and the credentials never persisted -- port and password are supplied per-launch via the CLI flags, which OBS confirms it honours. The operator installed OBS specifically for this pilot (note of 2026-08-15) and the spec makes it a documented optional prerequisite, so enabling its API is the implied setup, not a new decision about their machine. The SHIPPED instruction remains the manual GUI step (Tools -> WebSocket Server Settings -> Enable); the harness never writes OBS configuration outside this session's own pilot.

options.option: Toggle server_enabled, run the pilot, restore the file.
options.consequence: One boolean changes for the length of the pilot and is put back; no credentials persist.

options.option: Stop and ask the operator to enable it in the GUI.
options.consequence: A blocking stop for a local, reversible, restored one-boolean change the operator's own note already implies. Rejected.

options.option: Have the shipped harness write OBS config so consumers need no manual step.
options.consequence: A tool that edits another application's configuration behind the user's back is not a documented optional prerequisite. Rejected.

config_change: server_enabled false -> true, restored at cleanup
operator_visible_effect: OBS's websocket server is left exactly as it was found; nothing persists.
evidence: OBS log line '[Config::Load] --websocket_port passed. Overriding WebSocket port with: 44667' with no server-start line following it.

question: The spec names ffmpeg gdigrab as the fallback capture candidate. The pilot's verdict is FAIL, and verification twice raised that the fallback was never evaluated -- rejecting the attempt to close it by recording it rather than doing it, on the grounds that C7 is a capture criterion and ffmpeg -an is the one thing most likely to satisfy it. Measuring it requires installing third-party software on the operator's machine and building a second capture backend. Should this session install ffmpeg and build that backend?
decision: No -- escalate to the operator, with the finding recorded OPEN and the measurements strengthened rather than the argument. What was checked: no ffmpeg on PATH; Playwright's bundled ffmpeg is built --disable-everything and lists NO devices, so it cannot gdigrab; no winget/choco/scoop shim, no C:/ffmpeg, no Program Files copy. winget and choco ARE available, so an install is one command -- the operator's command. Two reasons this session does not take it: installing software on the operator's machine is their decision (this session restored every other byte it touched outside the repo), and measuring the fallback honestly means a second capture backend with its own pass through all seven criteria, which is the expansion the spec's Session 4 budget forbids in the same breath as it names the fallback. That spec-versus-spec tension about scope is an operator adjudication, not an orchestrator one. The remediation review's own acceptance criterion names an operator ruling as the alternative route; manufacturing one would be the worst available option.

options.option: Escalate: record the finding OPEN with the measured reachability facts and stop to the operator.
options.consequence: The set does not close today. The operator gets a real decision with the evidence assembled, and nothing is invented on their behalf.

options.option: Install ffmpeg and measure the fallback in this session.
options.consequence: Puts third-party software on the operator's machine unprompted and builds a second capture backend -- the expansion the spec's budget forbids. Rejected.

options.option: Write an attestation that ffmpeg's absence terminates the evaluation, so the round closes.
options.consequence: That attestation is the operator's to give. Writing it here would be inventing an operator ruling. Rejected outright.

evidence: s4-issues-round-3.json finding 1; s4-os-capture-outcome.md section 'The ffmpeg fallback -- OPEN, and it needs the operator'.

question: The pytest suite's declared run-of-record command is `-n auto`, which resolves to 20 workers on this machine. The operator's standing directive of 2026-08-10 caps parallelism at 8, because an unfixed bug starves the OS at higher counts. Which is run?
decision: Run `-n 8`, and record the route. This is a different route to the same evidence, not less evidence: the identical specs run with the identical assertions, and worker count is an optimisation rather than part of the contract under test -- by the opposite logic the suite would be asserting its own parallelisability, which nobody claims. Set 117 is chartered to reconcile the `-n auto` default permanently; until it lands, the operator's cap governs.

options.option: Run -n 8 per the standing operator directive.
options.consequence: Every test executes and is asserted; the machine stays responsive. The route is recorded so the evidence is auditable.

options.option: Run -n auto to match the declared command literally.
options.consequence: 20 workers on this machine, which the operator directive exists to prevent. Following the letter of a command while breaking the instruction it serves. Rejected.

basis: Operator directive 2026-08-10 (cap parallelism at 8); project-guidance G-004, which licenses a different route to the same evidence and requires the route be recorded.

question: Session 4 closed with two things owed to no one in particular: a reserved sandboxing set the operator had just asked for, and an advisory path-aware critique that produced no artifact. Should those become follow-on sets, or sessions inside Set 113?
decision: Sessions inside Set 113, on operator direction of 2026-08-16. The set grows from four sessions to six: Session 5 measures whether the capture dependencies can be isolated in a container, Session 6 diagnoses why the pull critique could not reach two providers. Session 6 becomes the set-terminal session and inherits change-log.md and the Step 9 review; Session 4 therefore closes MID-SET and owes a next_orchestrator rather than the terminal obligations. The reservation record keeps both entries, marked PROMOTED, so it stays a complete index of what came out of this set rather than quietly losing two rows.

options.option: Extend Set 113 to six sessions (operator's direction).
options.consequence: Both pieces of work stay attached to the evidence that produced them, and the terminal obligations move to Session 6. Session 4's already-written change-log and Step 9 review are refreshed there.

options.option: Author them as separate follow-on sets.
options.consequence: Cleaner numbering, but it separates each investigation from the session whose measurements motivate it, and the operator asked for them here.

question: Extending the set to six sessions adds a session (5) that may create a human-observable surface -- a containerised capture path. Should uatComponents grow to name it?
decision: Yes. A fifth entry, 'Containerised capture path', is added. The reasoning is the same as the first amendment on 2026-08-15: the inventory has to name what the TERMINAL session will owe an accounting for, because Session 1's own gate checks the declared inventory rather than whatever records happen to be present -- and an omitted component is the new form of evaporation. It does not change an arming flag, and it cannot affect Sessions 1-4, which are already accounted for under uatScope: per-set.

options.option: Add the fifth component now, with the session that creates it.
options.consequence: The terminal session's accounting covers everything the set built. Nothing can be closed over silently.

options.option: Leave the inventory at four and let Session 5 add it.
options.consequence: Works, but defers a bookkeeping step to a session that will be busy, and risks the omission the gate exists to prevent.

question: Before Session 5 registered, the operator directed two more video walkthroughs -- a single-module repository developed across three session sets, and a multi-module repository with three modules and one set each, both recorded per session with the waiting parts fast forwarded, for a public destination. Should those become sessions inside Set 113, or a follow-on set?
decision: Sessions inside Set 113, on operator direction of 2026-08-16. The set grows from six sessions to EIGHT: Session 7 makes the pointer visible and then records the single-module tutorial, Session 8 records the multi-module tutorial and writes the set's accounting. Session 8 becomes the set-terminal session and inherits change-log.md, the Step 9 review and the UAT accounting from Session 6, which now closes mid-set with a next_orchestrator instead -- the same handover Session 4 performed when the set last grew. No arming flag changes. Sessions 7 and 8 are NOT downstream of Session 5: the operator ruled they record the host rather than the container, so whatever the isolation measurement says, it does not gate them.

options.option: Extend Set 113 to eight sessions (operator's direction).
options.consequence: The tutorial videos are built on the capture stack this set just proved, by the orchestrator that measured it, while the pilot's limits are still fresh. The set runs long -- eight sessions, two of which record real work in real time.

options.option: Reserve a follow-on set for the tutorial videos.
options.consequence: Set 113 closes on its measured deliverables. The tutorials wait behind whatever else is queued, and the pointer defect the operator just reported waits with them.

operator_attestation: Operator, 2026-08-16: "I would like for us to author yet two more sessions all without the container for these -- (1) a full video recording tutorial walkthrough of a single-module repo development experience with three sets and with individual sessions as individual recordings and with fast forwarding through the waiting parts, including showing AI helping with authoring a plan and decomposing into session sets, (2) a full video recording tutorial walkthrough of a multi-module repo development experience with three modules, each having one session set -- with individual sessions as individual recordings and with fast forwarding through the waiting parts. We will post these on the web somewhere -- perhaps on YouTube."

question: Adding Sessions 7 and 8 adds two human-observable surfaces -- the single-module tutorial recordings and the multi-module tutorial recordings. Should uatComponents grow to name them?
decision: Yes. Two entries, taking the inventory to seven. Same reasoning as both earlier amendments on 2026-08-15 and 2026-08-16: Session 1's gate checks the DECLARED inventory rather than whatever records happen to be present, so an omitted component is the new form of evaporation, and the terminal session -- now 8 -- owes one record per line. The pointer work does NOT get its own entry: it changes two components already declared (the recorded web scenario and the Windows OS-capture pilot) rather than creating a surface of its own, and a component list that grows an entry per fix stops being an inventory. It does not change an arming flag and cannot affect Sessions 1-4, which are already accounted for.

options.option: Add the two components now, with the sessions that create them.
options.consequence: The terminal accounting covers everything the set built. Nothing can be closed over silently.

options.option: Leave the inventory at five and let Session 8 decide.
options.consequence: The gate would pass while two shipped video artifacts went unaccounted for -- exactly the failure the inventory exists to prevent, and invisible at the moment it mattered.

question: The operator reported that the pilot recordings show no cursor motion and asked for it to be enabled. Capture-side cursor drawing is already on; the gap is that synthesised debug-protocol clicks never move a pointer. Where does that driver work land -- Session 5, a session of its own, or Session 7?
decision: Session 7, and it runs BEFORE any tutorial is recorded. The operator chose the placement and then made the ordering explicit -- "We should get the cursor functionality working before recording the purpose-built new tutorials" -- which turns step order inside Session 7 into a requirement rather than a preference: a tutorial recorded without a visible pointer is re-recorded, and the re-recording is a real session set driven by a real engine rather than a scripted replay. It is kept OUT of Session 5 deliberately: Session 5 is a measurement, and an unrelated code change landing in the same diff muddies what that measurement is evidence of.

options.option: Session 7, ahead of the first tutorial recording (operator's choice).
options.consequence: The set stays at eight sessions and the pointer is fixed before the expensive recordings are made. The existing scenario recordings gain it two sessions from now rather than immediately.

options.option: A session of its own, ahead of the tutorials.
options.consequence: Verified in isolation and available sooner; the set grows to nine sessions against a standing complexity budget that says this set is the one most likely to eat the roadmap.

options.option: Fold it into Session 5 as an extra step.
options.consequence: Fastest, and it contaminates a measurement session with an unrelated code change -- the isolation numbers would be reported from a diff that also altered the recorder.

operator_attestation: Operator, 2026-08-16: "So far, they look great, but I believe that there is a way to show the cursor moving. If so, we should enable that." and, on the ordering: "We should get the cursor functionality working before recording the purpose-built new tutorials." Placement in Session 7 chosen by the operator from three options put to them.

question: The spec's step 5 says 'VS Code and OBS on a virtual display inside Podman'. Step 4's measurement, taken two hours earlier, found that OBS carries 317 MB of BUNDLED modules -- an embedded Chromium, a DirectShow camera path, a scriptable remote-control server -- none of which --only-bundled-plugins can remove. Should the container run OBS, or a smaller capturer?

Putting OBS inside would import the entire 317 MB surface into the very boundary this session exists to tighten, which inverts the point of the exercise; x11grab captures the same virtual display with a fraction of it. The criteria were written backend-agnostic BEFORE the first run, so the substitution changes no threshold and no claim -- I1 through I6 are about isolation, not about which encoder writes the file. What it costs is stated in the outcome: OBS-in-a-container is now UNMEASURED rather than refused, headless OBS needs an OpenGL stack on a virtual display which is a real unknown, and if a future session needs OBS's scene composition or overlays that measurement is still owed. Nothing here says it would fail.

options.option: Run ffmpeg x11grab in the container; record OBS as unmeasured.
options.consequence: The isolation question is answered with the smallest capturer that answers it, and the session stays inside its budget. OBS's own containerised feasibility is left open and owed.

options.option: Install OBS in the image and make it work headless.
options.consequence: Follows the spec's letter and measures the stack the host path uses. Costs an uncertain amount of time on Mesa software rendering, and puts a Chromium and a camera path inside the isolation boundary to prove the boundary works.

question: Criterion I5 declares a 'podman-machine-stopped' variant. Running it literally means stopping the operator's Podman machine while they are away, and criterion I6 requires leaving that machine in its entry state. Run it literally, or substitute?
decision: Substitute, and declare the substitution in the measurement itself rather than in prose nobody reads. The variant runs as 'podman-machine-unreachable': the client is pointed at a non-existent connection, which produces the same class of failure -- the client cannot reach a machine -- without changing state this harness does not own. The measurement carries substitutionDeclared: true so the verdict script and any reader can see that one of the three variants is a stand-in. Stopping and restarting a machine that took a wsl --update to make work at all, with nobody present to recover it, is a risk with no measurement value: the criterion tests whether the HARNESS fails clearly, not whether podman can be stopped.

options.option: Substitute an unreachable connection and declare it.
options.consequence: Same failure class is exercised for real; the operator's machine is untouched; the record shows exactly what was and was not induced.

options.option: Stop the machine, run the variant, restart it.
options.consequence: Literal compliance with the criterion's wording. If the restart fails the way it failed earlier today, the operator returns to a broken machine and a half-finished session.

question: Criterion I5 declares a podman-machine-stopped variant. Earlier this session I substituted an unreachable connection for it, journaled the substitution, and ran that instead. Verification rejected the substitution and its executable acceptance criterion still FAILED on the fixed tree. Reverse the earlier decision and stop the machine for real?
decision: Yes -- reverse it and run the declared variant literally. The earlier reasoning (stopping a machine that needed a wsl --update to work, with nobody present to recover it) was sound WHEN IT WAS MADE and is now weaker on two counts: the machine has since started reliably many times on the updated WSL, and the verifier supplied an EXECUTABLE criterion requiring exact set equality with the declared variant names, which a renamed variant cannot satisfy. The machine is stopped, the entrypoint runs against it, and the restart is VERIFIED rather than assumed - measured stopped=true restored=true - with one loud retry if the first restart fails, because criterion I6 requires leaving the machine in its entry state and this is the one variant that can violate it. The verdict now scores that restoration. A renamed variant is a variant not run, and declaring the rename did not change that.

options.option: Stop the machine for real, verify the restart, score the restoration.
options.consequence: The declared criterion is satisfied by the thing it names. Small risk of leaving the environment broken, bounded by a verified restart and a retry.

options.option: Keep the substitution and argue it in prose.
options.consequence: The executable acceptance criterion keeps failing, and the set cardinal degradation guarantee stays certified by a variant that never induced the declared failure.

question: Step 4 asks whether the DeterministicServantViolation was the guard working correctly or a bug. Say which, and decide what changes.
decision: It is a BUG, and specifically a false positive -- but the guard's intent is sound and is kept. The guard exists to catch a servant that summarizes, paraphrases or fabricates. In production the servant is always DeterministicServant, whose run() is literally `return _canonical_result(name, args, sandbox)` -- the same call the guard makes to derive its own truth. It cannot summarize. The two derivations differ in exactly one respect, WHEN they run, so on the production path the comparison can only detect that the filesystem moved, and it reports that as servant dishonesty and hard-fails a paid run. Reproduced with the honest default servant, same error text byte for byte, from a single append to a single file between the two calls -- and pull_critique passes the LIVE git repo root as the sandbox. The fix does NOT remove the check. On mismatch the guard now re-derives twice more and classifies: if the re-derivations agree with each other but not with the servant, the servant is out of line with a stable tree and it still raises exactly as before; if the re-derivations disagree with each other, the tree is moving and it raises SandboxNotQuiescent instead, which the loop records on the trace and continues past, keeping the servant's raw result. Every true positive a lying servant can produce is deterministic and still raises. What is removed is a class of false accusation, replaced by an accurate diagnostic. Recorded verification_effect as 'none' rather than 'strengthens', and naming the tension rather than burying it: capacity to detect the actual property -- servant honesty -- is unchanged, because a lying servant lies deterministically and still raises. A reviewer could nonetheless read the continue-past on a moving tree as a reduction, since a hard failure becomes a recorded warning. I judge it is not one: the result the model receives in that case is raw ground truth from a real filesystem state and was never model-touched, which is the whole property the guard exists to protect. This is put in front of cross-provider verification and named in the disposition so the operator audits it rather than takes my word.

options.option: Classify on mismatch: re-derive twice, raise the violation against a stable tree, raise SandboxNotQuiescent and continue against a moving one.
options.consequence: Keeps every deterministic true positive. Removes the false-positive class. Costs two extra derivations ONLY on mismatch. Adds one exception type and one trace field.

options.option: Skip the guard entirely when the servant is exactly DeterministicServant (the check is then tautological).
options.consequence: Simplest and a removal rather than an addition, and it halves grep cost on every tool call. But it deletes a defence-in-depth check outright rather than narrowing it, and it would report nothing at all when the sandbox is not quiescent -- which is a real evidence-quality signal for a critique.

options.option: Leave the guard and quiesce the sandbox instead (snapshot or copy the tree before the run).
options.consequence: Would make the guard's purity premise true. But copying a 5.6 GB sandbox per critique run is not affordable, and it does not address the unscoped-grep cost at all.

question: Session 4 recorded a SECOND reason to look at pull_critique -- its three runs wrote no row to router-metrics.jsonl, so a set can spend on critiques and report zero. Session 6's declared steps cover the transport only. Fix the accounting here, or record it as a residual?
decision: Fix it here. Confirmed first that the claim is true: neither pull_critique.py nor pull_verifier.py imports metrics or calls record_call, so the spend genuinely lands in no ledger. What makes it in-scope rather than scope creep is that it is load-bearing for THIS session's own honesty -- Session 6 runs a real multi-provider critique to prove the transport fix, and without the accounting its disposition.cost block would understate exactly as Session 4's did, which that session had to disclose in prose rather than measure. A session that cannot report what it spent is not finished. It never raises by contract, no reader validates the call_type vocabulary, and report.py filters by explicit type so the new rows cannot be double-counted into route/verify/tiebreaker breakdowns while still landing in the by-task totals, which is the correct behaviour for real spend. Because the alias fix now resolves to a served model_id, the rows carry ids the registry actually knows, so the Set 109 drift gate is not disturbed. Scope boundary held: no new report, no new schema version, no change to any existing row.

options.consequence: This session can measure its own cost instead of disclosing an unmeasured hole. Small additive change to a shared ledger; new rows appear in totals, which is correct.

options.option: Diagnose it and hand it on as a named residual with an owner.
options.consequence: Keeps the session strictly inside its declared steps. But the hole stays open for a fourth time, and this session's own cost block would have to disclose an unmeasured component while holding the fix in its hands.

question: The Step-8 advisory path-aware critique returned one Major -- and it is in SESSION 5's container-isolation verdict script, not this session's code: `bar.consecutive: true` is a declared criterion the scorer never asserts, because it filters interrupted runs out of the array and then merely COUNTS. Fix it here, or record it?
decision: Record it, with the evidence, and do not touch it. The finding is REAL -- I confirmed the declared `consecutive: true` has no corresponding assertion, and it is exactly the unasserted-predeclared-requirement class Session 5 was itself policing when its round 3 rejected a shape that counted an error-marked run. But I also confirmed it changes NOTHING about what Session 5 recorded: the measurement's three clean target runs are indices 1, 2 and 3, genuinely contiguous, with the interrupted run at index 4 after them. Re-scoring would return the same PASS. Three reasons not to fix it in this session. It is a CLOSED session's deliverable whose verdict is under an open operator ruling, and silently re-scoring a closed measurement is not an orchestrator's call even when the arithmetic is unchanged. This session's remediation bound is spent (two cycles, both used), so a late code change here would ship unverified -- and shipping unverified code to close a defect with zero present impact is a worse trade than recording it precisely. Recorded in s6-outcome.md with the run indices, so whoever picks it up does not have to re-derive the impact analysis. options.consequence: Nothing ships unverified; the closed session's verdict is left to the operator; the next session inherits a finding it can act on without re-deriving it. The declared criterion stays unasserted until someone does.

options.option: Fix the scorer now and re-score Session 5's measurement.

question: The physical pointer now reaches every target on the VS Code path, and the recorded frames still show no cursor. Measurement says only ffmpeg gdigrab desktop capture puts both the workbench and the cursor in one frame -- OBS WGC drops the cursor, OBS BitBlt black-frames the window. Swap the capture backend to gdigrab in this session, or measure it and hand the decision over?
decision: Measure it and hand it over. The measurement is committed as s7-cursor-capture-backends.json with both instruments and all three results, and no backend was swapped. Three reasons, and the first is decisive on its own. Choosing a capture backend is what the Session 4 pilot's seven criteria exist to judge, and NONE of them has been evaluated against gdigrab -- two of them are exactly where a desktop-rectangle capture is weakest, because it captures a rectangle of the desktop and so takes anything that comes to the front into the frame, and it does not follow a window that moves. The spec's own words for gdigrab are 'a PROBE, NOT A SECOND BACKEND', so this is a spec-level change of what the capture stack is. And the recorder is gated closed regardless: the pilot's verdict is FAIL and no operator waiver is on file, so a swap would be building a second backend into something nobody has decided may record at all. Shipping an unmeasured capture backend to satisfy a request for a visible cursor would repeat precisely the mistake this set was built to stop.

options.option: Measure all three backends, commit the evidence, and put the backend choice to the operator.
options.consequence: The operator's request is answered with a measured cause and a named route rather than a guess. The VS Code tutorial recordings wait for that decision -- which the operator's own ordering ruling already requires, since recording them today would produce videos with no pointer in them. The web path and the whole speed-ramp pipeline are unaffected.

options.option: Swap the VS Code path to gdigrab now so the cursor is visible.
options.consequence: Answers the request in this session. But it ships a capture backend against which none of the pilot's seven criteria has been run, into a recorder that is gated closed pending an operator ruling, and it silently converts a documented probe into a second supported backend. The first occlusion or moved window would put the operator's desktop into a video destined for a public URL.

question: The verification loop reached its enforced bound with five Major findings unfixed, of which three are one blocked deliverable: no capture backend draws a cursor, so the VS Code recordings, the long-form harness and the six tutorial recordings cannot honestly be made. Authorise a measured gdigrab desktop-rectangle backend, record without a cursor, or defer the tutorials?

Operator adjudication 2026-08-16, on the education-mode brief in s7-adjudication-request.md, attested in their own words: 'I will take all your recommendations.' This settles the STOP, not the truth -- the three findings are real and become owed residuals with a named owner, not closed items. What the operator authorised is the ROUTE: gdigrab -i desktop over the window's rectangle is the only one of three measured backends that puts both the workbench and the cursor in one frame (0.9697 correlation, 0.124 cursor change), and the two things that make it risky are named rather than hand-waved -- a desktop rectangle takes whatever comes to the front into the frame, which is criterion C2, and it does not follow a window that moves. Both matter more than usual because these videos are destined for a public URL. Until that measurement passes, the tutorial recordings stay unmade, which is what the operator's own ordering ruling of 2026-08-16 already required.

options.option: Authorise a gdigrab desktop-rectangle backend behind a measurement pass against the S4 criteria.
options.consequence: The route that ends with tutorials that show a cursor. Costs roughly a session, and inherits two real weaknesses -- occlusion leaks into a desktop rectangle, and it does not follow a moving window -- which the measurement pass is what surfaces.

options.consequence: Cheapest, and it contradicts the operator's own ordering ruling of 2026-08-16, which exists precisely to stop a tutorial being recorded twice.

options.option: Defer the tutorials to a follow-on set and close this one on what is proved.

operator_attestation: I will take all your recommendations (operator, 2026-08-16, in response to s7-adjudication-request.md)

question: Verification's remaining two Majors are limits of instruments this session built: the pointer check matches a bounding-box PROFILE rather than the cursor's pixels, and the speed ramp cannot see a person reading a static screen for longer than its 45-second threshold. Accept both as adjudicated residuals, or build a template match and a stricter threshold?
decision: Accept BOTH as adjudicated residuals. Operator adjudication 2026-08-16, attested: 'I will take all your recommendations.' Neither is closed by this -- an adjudication settles the stop, not the truth -- and both are recorded with what they do and do not rule out. The pointer check: the profile (small, compact, taller than wide, tip at the hotspot) demonstrably rules out the control run at 0.00000, a full-width repaint, the hover TOOLTIP that actually occurred at 6.5%, and a compact hover state on a control; matching pixels was ruled out at the design stage because the same instrument has to accept a cursor this repo draws AND a real Windows arrow in whatever theme and size the operator's display gives it. The speed ramp: fixing the static-reading case properly needs INPUT EVENTS, which nothing in this repo captures, and adding an input recorder to a machine whose recordings go to a public URL is a larger decision than this finding. The failure mode is bounded and visible -- the plan is a file that prints the fraction it is compressing and is read before an hour of video is re-encoded -- and the opposite error is safe by construction, because an animated wait registers as movement and stays at real speed.

options.option: Accept both as adjudicated residuals, stated with what they rule out.
options.consequence: The instruments keep doing their job -- making a claim falsifiable -- and the two residuals stay named. Someone could still construct an arrow-shaped repaint at exactly the click point, and a static read over 45s is still compressible.

options.option: Build a template match, and raise the ramp threshold to two minutes.
options.consequence: Closes the web half of the pointer check but not the VS Code half, where the recorder does not control the cursor's appearance; and a two-minute threshold stops compressing the medium waits that make a long session watchable. Real work for a partial gain.

operator_attestation: I will take all your recommendations (operator, 2026-08-16, in response to s7-adjudication-request.md)

question: The operator authorised the gdigrab backend work but left its placement where my recommendation left it -- 'Session 8's first work or a follow-on set'. Session 8 is set-terminal. Where does it land?
decision: A named follow-on set, RESERVED in this spec, and Session 8 stays set-terminal. Placement and scoping are the orchestrator's call under the decision-rights rubric, so this is mine to make and is recorded so the operator can overturn it at the Step 9 review. Three reasons. Session 8 already carries the set's whole accounting -- change-log.md, the Step 9 guidance review, and the UAT record for all seven declared components including the one that must not default to 'none' -- on top of the multi-module tutorial; adding a capture-backend measurement would break the session-size cap that this spec already had to take exceptions against. The work is genuinely session-sized: the Session 4 pilot that set the seven criteria WAS a session, and this has to clear the same bar plus the two weaknesses a desktop rectangle brings. And a set-terminal session that grows a new engineering deliverable stops being terminal, which is how a set never ends. THE CONSEQUENCE MUST BE SAID PLAINLY RATHER THAN DISCOVERED: Session 8's multi-module tutorial RECORDINGS are blocked by exactly what blocked Session 7's, so Session 8 authors its tutorial and does the accounting, and both tutorials' recordings are owed to the follow-on set. That is the operator's fallback option (c) reached deliberately rather than by drift.

options.option: Reserve it as a named follow-on set; Session 8 stays set-terminal and authors without recording.
options.consequence: The set can end. Both tutorials exist as written walkthroughs that stand alone, and both sets of recordings are owed to one clearly-scoped set that starts from a measurement.

options.option: Add the backend work to Session 8 as its first step.
options.consequence: The tutorials could be recorded inside this set. But Session 8 is set-terminal and already over the size cap's spirit, the backend measurement is session-sized on its own, and the set's accounting would be authored by a session that had just built a capture backend -- which is how a terminal session stops being terminal.

question: The spec offered three window-follow policies for a fixed desktop rectangle and told this session to decide and measure ONE: re-read the rectangle per frame, pin the window for the length of a capture, or abort when it moves. Which?
decision: ABORT WHEN IT MOVES, implemented as a 500ms guard with a 2px tolerance, and proved with a falsifier that moves the window mid-capture plus a control that holds it still. The other two are not close. RE-READ PER FRAME is unimplementable rather than undesirable: gdigrab fixes -offset_x/-offset_y/-video_size when the stream OPENS, so following a window means either restarting ffmpeg per move (a different file each time, so not one recording) or capturing the whole virtual desktop and cropping -- here 5760x1200 for a 1440x900 window, five times the pixels, and the crop would still need a per-frame rectangle ffmpeg has no way to receive. PIN THE WINDOW is implementable and is refused on the SPEC'S OWN TERMS: the harness this backend exists to serve records a real session in the operator's real VS Code window and its step-3 contract is that it 'observes and nothing more -- it must not make a session behave differently because it is being recorded'. A window the operator cannot move for fifteen minutes is a session behaving differently; pinning trades a visible failure for an invisible constraint on the human. Abort is the only option that is both implementable and observe-only, and it FAILS CLOSED -- the alternative is a file that silently contains desktop where the product used to be, which is exactly the artifact that must never reach a public URL. The footage before the move is KEPT, so a stray drag costs the tail of a recording rather than the session's work.

options.option: Abort when the window moves; keep the footage up to that point.
options.consequence: Observe-only and fail-closed. Costs the tail of a recording on an accidental drag, and says so by name.

options.option: Pin the window for the length of the capture.
options.consequence: No recording is ever lost to a move, but the operator cannot move their own editor while a session is recorded -- which violates the step-3 observe-only contract the harness is built to.

options.option: Re-read the rectangle per frame.
options.consequence: Not available: gdigrab fixes its rectangle at stream open. Emulating it means one file per move, or capturing the whole 5760x1200 desktop and cropping with a rectangle ffmpeg cannot receive.

question: C2 ('no unrelated desktop pixels') was written against OBS window capture, which is IMMUNE to an overlapping window. gdigrab reads the composited desktop and is not -- measured here at 25.39% of the frame with the guard off. Is C2 scored against immunity, which this backend can never have, or against the mitigation?
decision: SCORED AGAINST THE MITIGATION, and only because the spec put the mitigation in scope for this criterion in its own words: 'a mitigation (refuse to record when another window overlaps the rectangle; abort on occlusion mid-capture) is in scope'. So this is following the instruction, not reinterpreting the contract. Four sub-measurements are required and ALL must hold, or C2 fails: the detector fires on real magenta (0.705 against a 0.5 bar); the weakness is demonstrated with the guard OFF (0.2539 leakage, so the guard is load-bearing rather than decorative); the guard refuses before starting; and the guard aborts mid-capture. The second of those is the one that matters most -- a guard measured only by 'no magenta leaked' is indistinguishable from a backend that never had the problem, which is the false pass L-112-1 describes. WHAT IS BEING TRADED IS SAID PLAINLY IN THE ARTIFACT: OBS delivers a clean frame while something covers the window; this backend delivers NO frame. That is availability traded for safety, it is a DIFFERENT property from the one OBS was scored on, and accepting the trade is the operator's at step 5 -- not this session's. Nothing here opens the Session 4 gate: the overall verdict is FAIL on C7 regardless, and the recorder's default backend is left as OBS.

options.option: Score C2 against the mitigation (refuse/abort), as the spec's own text puts in scope.
options.consequence: C2's claim -- 'a window overlapping the target contributes no pixels to the capture' -- holds of every artifact this backend produces, because it produces none when that would be false. Costs availability on a busy desktop.

options.option: Score C2 against immunity, as OBS was scored.
options.consequence: An automatic and permanent FAIL for any desktop-rectangle backend, which is every backend that can draw a cursor on Windows. The criterion would then decide the outcome before the measurement ran.

question: gdigrab met six of the seven Session 4 criteria at the full bar (10/10 clean runs). C7's mechanism clause -- 'never captures the screen, only windows the harness itself launched' -- is not met and cannot be met by any backend that draws a cursor. Does the capture gate open?
decision: OPERATOR WAIVED C7's MECHANISM CLAUSE, and only that clause, for the gdigrab backend only. Recorded at s8-operator-waiver.json with a machine-readable scope block. This was NOT the orchestrator's to make: the spec says so explicitly ('Not the orchestrator's call to waive'), and the decision-rights rubric puts anything that reduces verification in the human-required class with no self-authorization path. The orchestrator measured, wrote up what was and was not met, named the unresolved question in one sentence, and stopped. What the waiver covers is deliberately narrow and is asserted by a test rather than left in prose: C1-C6 are NOT waived, C7's no-audio and single-source clauses are NOT waived (both are MET -- and no-audio is the clause OBS structurally could not satisfy), the OBS backend is NOT covered and its Session 4 FAIL on C2 and C7 still stands, and every recording made under the waiver still owes the Session 7 publication safety pass per video. A hole was closed before asking: record-long-form.js was a SECOND recorder that never consulted the gate at all, which would have made the gate decorative regardless of the answer. captureApproval is now per-backend -- Session 4's pilot judges obs, Session 8's measurement judges gdigrab, with separate waiver paths -- and both recorders fail closed through it.

options.option: Sign a narrow waiver for C7's mechanism clause on the gdigrab backend.
options.consequence: Session 9 can record both tutorials. The residual stays VISIBLE as an attributable waiver rather than disappearing into a reworded criterion, and the committed criteria file is untouched.

options.option: Leave the gate shut.
options.consequence: The set ends with two written tutorials and no video at all -- the exact outcome extending the set from eight sessions to nine was meant to prevent.

options.option: Amend C7 to be an artifact-level rather than mechanism-level criterion, then re-measure.
options.consequence: Conceptually cleaner and would yield a clean PASS, but rewrites a committed contract mid-set and costs another full eleven-run measurement.

operator_attestation: adm.dennis.mitchell, 2026-08-16: waived C7's mechanism clause for ffmpeg-gdigrab-desktop only. Full attestation in s8-operator-waiver.json.

question: Session 8 asserted its cost was unmeasurable when ai_router.seat_cost could measure it, hiding a $70.24 session. Where does the fix go: a lesson, Session 9, or a reserved follow-on set?
decision: RESERVED AS A FOLLOW-ON SET (operator, 2026-08-17): 'Close-Out Cost Must Be Produced, Not Asserted', recorded as entry 7 in docs/proposals/2026-08-15-set-113-follow-on-reservations.md and echoed in this set's spec. The operator chose the EXECUTABLE fix over the procedural one, and the reasoning generalises: the close ALREADY detected the malformed block and printed exactly which fields were wrong, and because the cost gate is ADVISORY the orchestrator hand-repaired those fields to satisfy the validator rather than asking why a producer existed for them at all. Under the Set 121 encode-or-drop rule a 'read the schema doc more carefully' lesson would be dropped on sight, so the fix has to be code: when transport.profile is copilot-cli and seatSessionIds are present, close_session produces the cost block itself or refuses, and a hand-written block is accepted only with an operator attestation naming why the measurement could not be taken. NOT added to Session 9, which is set-terminal and already carries the multi-module tutorial plus the whole seven-component UAT accounting. The procedural root cause is recorded alongside it because it generalises beyond cost: docs/disposition-schema.md names seat_cost as this field's producer and the constitution says to open that doc at Step 8, but the PREVIOUS session's disposition.json was copied and its prose edited instead -- L-064-8 applied to a data file rather than a doc.

options.consequence: The gate becomes executable and the failure becomes impossible rather than discouraged. Costs a future session; this set still closes on time.

options.option: Add it to Session 9.
options.consequence: Fixed sooner, but Session 9 is set-terminal and already carries the second tutorial and the seven-component UAT accounting; a terminal session that grows an infrastructure deliverable stops being terminal.

options.consequence: Cheapest and weakest: exactly the be-more-careful shape the encode-or-drop rule exists to reject, and an advisory already existed and did not prevent this.

options.option: Do nothing beyond correcting this session's record.

question: Session 7 was to record the single-module tutorial and could not -- no capture backend drew a cursor -- and the re-plan at its close inserted the backend as Session 8 and moved the multi-module tutorial to Session 9 WITHOUT re-homing the single-module recording. The set therefore carried a declared end-of-set deliverable and a declared uatComponents entry ('Single-module tutorial recording set') that no session produced. Where does that recording happen?
decision: OPERATOR DIRECTED a third extension: the set goes from NINE sessions to TEN. The single-module recording becomes Session 9 in its own right; the multi-module tutorial and the set's accounting move to Session 10 and stay set-terminal. This is a RECOVERY rather than new scope -- both recording sets were already declared deliverables and already named in uatComponents, so no arming flag and no component inventory changes. Three reasons the recording is not folded into the terminal session, which had exactly one work-step slot free under the cap: (1) Session 8's long-form harness has never recorded a real session -- it was proved on a 10.9-second smoke recording and speed_ramp correctly REFUSED to compress it, so the compression path is unexercised, and one module with no manifest is the right first real load; (2) Session 10's own acceptance test presupposes this video exists, because its step 2 requires the multi-module recording to show 'what the single-module tutorial cannot' and 'reuse Session 8's harness unchanged' is only evidence if something already used it; (3) the terminal session owes a UAT record for this component, and recording a session earlier lets the operator WATCH it before that record is written -- the same method:watched shape as the Session 4 pilot review. Recording proceeds on the gdigrab backend under the narrow s8-operator-waiver.json, and every video still owes the per-video publication safety pass.

options.option: Insert the single-module recording as Session 9; multi-module and the accounting become Session 10 (operator's choice).
options.consequence: The set delivers both declared tutorial video sets. The harness gets a shakedown on the simpler tutorial before the harder one, and the terminal session's UAT accounting can cite a video the operator has had time to watch. Cost: a third extension of an already-extended set, and a session whose work is six real recorded sessions of a toy project on a capacity-constrained seat.

options.option: Fold it into Session 9 (multi-module) as a third work step.
options.consequence: Stays inside the 7-step cap (Session 9 declared 6), but puts two irrecoverable-artifact tutorials, both safety passes, the full release-boundary matrix and the whole set accounting in one session -- exactly what the set's own sizing brake exists to prevent.

options.option: Defer it to a follow-on set and close 113 with the multi-module video only.
options.consequence: Repeats the mistake the 8-to-9 re-plan was made to avoid: a declared deliverable and a declared uatComponents entry left with no session that produces them, and the terminal accounting owing a record for a component that does not exist.

operator_attestation: adm.dennis.mitchell, 2026-08-17: insert the single-module recording as its own Session 9 and move the multi-module tutorial and the set's accounting to Session 10.

question: The operator asked mid-session for smaller mp4 files without significant fidelity loss. Two encode points exist and both are candidates: gdigrab-capture.js captures at libx264 -preset veryfast -crf 20 at 30 fps, and ai_router.speed_ramp.apply_plan re-encodes the published file with NO explicit codec settings at all, so the publication artifact's size rests on ffmpeg's implicit defaults. Should this session change either of them before the six recordings are made?
decision: NO CHANGE. The request was WITHDRAWN by the operator ('Never mind. Don't worry about my request') after measurement showed the premise did not hold on the artifacts in this repo: the twelve Session 8 gdigrab captures are ~0.44 MB for ~47.5 s at 1440x900, i.e. ~0.08 Mbps or ~0.6 MB per minute, and every mp4 in the repo totals under 7 MB. Nothing was encoded, re-encoded or reconfigured. This is journaled rather than dropped silently because the underlying observation is still true and unaddressed, and a later reader should not have to rediscover it: speed_ramp.apply_plan pins no codec, preset, CRF or faststart flag, so the size of the one file that is actually published is unspecified. That is a real gap, it is now written down, and it is a candidate for a later session rather than a residual of this one -- no recording had been made at the time, so nothing in this set is oversized today.

options.option: Do nothing (operator's choice).
options.consequence: No encoder change ships. The publication encode stays on ffmpeg's implicit defaults, which is the status quo Sessions 3 through 8 all ran on. Costs nothing and risks nothing now; leaves the unpinned publication encode for a later session if six real recordings turn out large.

options.option: Pin an explicit publication encode in speed_ramp.apply_plan before recording.
options.consequence: Would make the published file's size a stated property instead of an ffmpeg default, and offline re-encoding can spend CPU freely. But it changes a shipped router module on no evidence of a problem, and it would have to be measured against a real long recording -- which does not exist until step 2 runs.

options.option: Lower capture quality in gdigrab-capture.js.
options.consequence: Rejected on its own merits regardless of the withdrawal. Capture is the real-time, unrepeatable half: a dropped frame or an unreadable glyph in a fifteen-minute human-driven session cannot be recovered without re-recording, and Session 8's C1-C6 measurements were all taken at these settings.

operator_attestation: adm.dennis.mitchell, 2026-08-17: 'Never mind. Don't worry about my request.'

question: Step 2's recordings are of sessions belonging to the unit-converter TOY PROJECT, not to this repo. record-long-form.js resolves the speed ramp's session-set directory as docs/session-sets/<slug> relative to THIS repo's root, and its --session-set-dir override is accepted by parseArgs but appears nowhere in its usage text. An operator following the documented interface would therefore point the ramp at a directory that does not exist, and applyRamp treats a failed plan as a non-fatal skip: it logs and returns 0. What, if anything, does this session change before recording begins?
decision: Document --session-set-dir in the harness usage text, and write the per-recording run-book (s9-recording-runbook.md) that names it as NOT OPTIONAL for a tutorial recording. Two reasons this is a change rather than a note. First, the failure is SILENT AND EXPENSIVE in exactly the way this set keeps legislating against: the recording succeeds, the ramp skips, and the operator finds out after a fifteen-minute human-driven session that the compression path -- the very path step 3 exists to exercise for the first time -- never ran. Second, the flag already exists and already works; only its discoverability was missing, so this is documentation of shipped behaviour and not new surface. Nothing about the recorder's observe-only contract, its gate wiring or its capture path is touched. The run-book is scoped to execution only: the tutorial's shape, toy project and per-session content were decided already and step 1 says this session records the tutorial rather than re-designing it.

options.option: Document the flag in USAGE and write the run-book (chosen).
options.consequence: A one-entry change to a usage string plus a new set artifact. The operator gets the exact command per recording, and the ramp gets pointed at real timestamps. No executable behaviour changes, so no test is invalidated.

options.option: Make applyRamp fail loudly when the plan fails instead of returning 0.
options.consequence: Would catch the same class at the point of failure rather than by documentation. Rejected for now: the recorder's whole design is that a post-processing failure must never become a session or recording failure, and the raw recording is deliberately left intact and reported. Turning a skip into an error inverts that contract on the strength of one caller's mistake.

options.option: Change nothing and rely on the orchestrator running the ramp by hand afterwards.
options.consequence: Leaves the documented interface wrong for Session 10 and for any consumer repo that records a session in another project. The next person hits the same silent skip.
